text: You've learned the definition, built a Bell state with real gates, drawn the classical-versus-quantum line, and seen the numeric test that proves entanglement is real. Now it's time to apply all four together.

Problem one: is ket-00 plus ket-01 plus ket-10 minus ket-11, over 2, entangled? Having four terms proves nothing by itself — the factoring test alone settles it. Matching coefficients requires a-c equal a-d, which forces c equal d; and b-c equal negative b-d, which forces c equal negative d. Together those force d to be zero — but zero d makes b-d zero too, contradicting the required negative one-half. Contradiction. This state is entangled.

Problem two: ket-01 plus ket-10 over root 2 is the Bell state Psi-plus. The same factoring test hits a contradiction, so it's entangled. But measuring it gives a different pattern than Phi-plus: if qubit 1 comes out 0, qubit 2 is guaranteed 1 — the opposite, not the same. If qubit 1 is 1, qubit 2 is guaranteed 0. Perfect anti-correlation: P of 01 and P of 10 are each 0.5, while P of 00 and P of 11 are exactly zero.

Problem three: a colleague says two classical coins could explain Phi-plus's correlation. They're partially right and mostly missing the point. If the only experiment is single-basis measurement, a classical script reproduces the numbers perfectly — that part is correct. Their mistake is concluding entanglement is never distinguishable from a classical script. Once you measure at multiple angles, the entangled pair gives a CHSH value of 2.828, while no local hidden-variable script can exceed 2. That multi-basis gap, confirmed by real experiments, is the precise answer.

Problem four: spot the error in 'measuring qubit 1 instantly tells you qubit 2's value, so information traveled faster than light.' The error is treating 'I can now predict your result' as 'I caused your result.' Nothing travels between the qubits at measurement time — qubit 2, measured on its own, still shows the same 50/50 statistics it always would. The prediction only becomes useful once someone physically compares both results, which requires ordinary, slower-than-light communication.
Chapter 5 turns to the no-cloning theorem: why you can't copy an unknown qubit, and what that restriction makes possible for teleportation and cryptography.
